Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search surfaced a clearly authoritative development, moving this to the full path. Burundi's National Assembly adopted a comprehensive personal data protection law (Loi N°1/03 du 10 mars 2026) on 15 January 2026, promulgated 10 March 2026, per the ARCT (telecoms regulator) official portal and corroborated by Data Protection Africa and independent trackers. The law restricts cross-border transfers of personal and sensitive/biometric data to destinations without adequate protection or approved safeguards, and creates a data protection authority whose detailed powers await an implementing decree (not yet identified). This is a transfer-adequacy regime rather than an explicit blanket mandate to store data within Burundi's borders, so its fit against this variable's scale (which is framed around in-country storage mandates) is genuinely ambiguous — it could reasonably be read as level 3 (sectoral/emerging) or level 4 (comprehensive). A prior UNECA digital-trade profile (undated, pre-2026) explicitly stated Burundi had no cross-border data transfer or localisation measures at all, confirming this is a new development. Flagged for human review to confirm the best-fit code given the enforcement authority is not yet operational.
revised_comments: Burundi enacted its first comprehensive personal data protection law (Loi N°1/03 du 10 mars 2026) in March 2026, which restricts cross-border transfers of personal and sensitive data to jurisdictions without adequate protection or approved safeguards, and establishes an independent data protection authority under the Ministry of Digital Economy, though the authority's detailed operating mandate awaits an implementing decree. Prior to this law, data protection existed only through scattered sectoral confidentiality provisions in banking, health and telecommunications legislation, with no general cross-border data transfer or localisation measures.

Definition: The presence and tier quality of commercial/colocation data center facilities operating in the country. Commercial data centers provide the physical infrastructure for hosting cloud services, content delivery, and enterprise applications domestically.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited source was fetched and does not support the stated score: Inflect itself lists two commercial data centre/colocation facilities in Bujumbura (Lacell SU's "Smart Burundi" and the Burundi Backbone System), and the original Comments field even names Lacell as a facility while scoring 'No commercial data centers'. Cross-checked against DataCenterJournal and Data Center Platform, which independently list the same two small-scale facilities. No Tier III or higher facility, and no hyperscale or major colocation operator (e.g. Raxio, Africa Data Centres, Teraco) presence was found. This matches Value Code 2 (small-scale facilities only, Tier I-II) rather than Code 1 (no commercial data centers).
revised_comments: Burundi has a small number of commercial/colocation facilities in Bujumbura — Lacell SU's "Smart Burundi" site and the Burundi Backbone System — but no Tier III or higher facility and no hyperscale or major regional colocation operator presence. Direct cloud on-ramps to AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure are absent locally, with traffic typically routed via Nairobi.

redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light-check search surfaced a clearly authoritative World Bank World Development Indicators figure (EG.ELC.RNEW.ZS: Renewable electricity output, % of total), moving this to the full path. World Bank data (mirrored consistently across two independent aggregators) puts Burundi's renewable share of electricity output at 61.30% in 2021, the latest year for which WDI reports data (last updated February 2026, with no newer figure published, consistent with Burundi's small hydropower-dominated generation mix). This falls within the 50-74% band, corresponding to Value Code 4.
revised_comments: Renewables (predominantly hydropower) accounted for 61.3% of Burundi's total electricity output in 2021, per World Bank World Development Indicators (EG.ELC.RNEW.ZS), the most recent year for which data are available. This is down from a peak of 100% in 2000, reflecting the country's growing reliance on thermal generation to address chronic supply shortfalls.

Definition: The maturity of the country's technology startup ecosystem, based on the number of tech startups, venture capital activity, accelerators/incubators, and the presence of a supportive ecosystem. Africa's startup scene is well-documented by trackers like Partech, Disrupt Africa, and Briter Bridges.
Value Name: Nascent (very few tech startups, no visible VC activity)
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited Partech report was fetched and is a continent-wide publication with no Burundi-specific data, so it does not directly evidence the score, though its overall finding (African VC concentrated in a handful of larger markets) is consistent with a nascent Burundi ecosystem. A more specific source, Dealroom.co's Burundi country profile, tracks only 3 startups nationally with $0 disclosed VC invested and a combined enterprise value of just $120K (2019-2025 window), ranking Burundi 43rd of tracked African markets. Local entrepreneurship-support initiatives exist (BujaHub, Orange Corners Burundi founded 2024, Maison de l'Entrepreneur incubator since 2008) but there is no visible VC deal activity or scaled tech startup base. This confirms Value Code 1.
revised_comments: Burundi's tech startup ecosystem remains nascent, with Dealroom tracking only around three startups nationally and no disclosed venture capital investment as of 2025. A small number of entrepreneurship-support initiatives operate in Bujumbura, including BujaHub, Orange Corners Burundi (launched 2024) and the longer-standing Maison de l'Entrepreneur incubator, but there is no visible institutional VC activity or funded scale-up pipeline.

revised_comments: Burundi's developer community is very small, comprising a handful of low-activity groups such as Rundi Dev Community, GDG Bujumbura and the GDSC chapter at Bujumbura International University, each with only a handful of GitHub followers and public repositories. redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited source was fetched and does not support the score: it is a general TAICEP/Scholaro conference slide deck on Burundi's history and credential evaluation, containing no information on ICT or STEM tertiary education. Direct searches of university websites found at least three institutions offering dedicated ICT/computer science programmes: the Université du Burundi's Faculté des Sciences de l'Ingénieur (TIC department, offering a Bachelor's and Master's in Génie Informatique/Réseaux et Télécoms), Bujumbura Christian University's Faculty of Science and Technology (Computer Network Management and Software Engineering departments), and Université du Lac Tanganyika's Faculté d'Informatique (five specialisation tracks including Génie Informatique, Génie Logiciel, Ingénierie des Réseaux and Télécommunications). This is well above the '<2 institutions' threshold for Value Code 1 and better matches Value Code 3 (several institutions, growing enrolment), though exact enrolment figures were not available to confirm the 'growing enrolment' qualifier.
revised_comments: At least three Burundian universities offer dedicated tertiary ICT and computer science programmes: the Université du Burundi's Faculté des Sciences de l'Ingénieur (Bachelor's and Master's degrees in Génie Informatique and Réseaux et Télécoms), Bujumbura Christian University's Faculty of Science and Technology (Computer Network Management and Software Engineering), and Université du Lac Tanganyika's Faculté d'Informatique, which offers five ICT specialisation tracks including software engineering, computer engineering, network engineering and telecommunications. Enrolment figures for these programmes are not published.
